modules.title: Hello, C
modules.summary: Your first programs. What main() is, how printf prints text, and how to read the compiler's complaints.

steps.title: Your first program
hints: The function that prints text is spelled `printf` (print formatted).

steps.title: Printing your own text
steps.text:
Whatever is between the double quotes is printed exactly. The quotes themselves are not printed.

Note the `;` at the end of the statement. In C, statements end with a semicolon, like a period ends a sentence.

**Your turn:** make the program print exactly:

```
I am learning C
```
hints: Type the sentence between the quotes. Capital letters and spaces matter.

steps.title: Several lines
steps.text:
Each `printf` call continues where the last one stopped. Only `\n` moves to a new line, so these two calls:

```c
printf("Ready, ");
printf("set\n");
```

print `Ready, set` on a single line.

**Your turn:** write a program that prints these three lines:

```
Counter-Strike
is a game
about aim
```
hints: Add one `printf` per line. Each one needs `\n` at the end of the text.
The second line is `printf("is a game\n");`

tests.name: Output
tests.expect:
Counter-Strike
is a game
about aim

steps.title: Escape sequences
steps.text:
Some characters can't be typed directly inside a string, so C uses **escape sequences** that start with a backslash:

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `\n` | new line |
| `\t` | tab |
| `\"` | a double quote |
| `\\` | a backslash |

**Your turn:** print this line exactly, including the quotes:

```
She said "gg" and left
```
hints: A plain `"` would end the string early. Write `\"` for each quote you want printed.

steps.title: Comments and reading errors
steps.text:
Comments are notes for humans. The compiler ignores them.

```c
// a comment runs to the end of the line
/* this kind can span
   several lines */
```

When the code is wrong, the compiler tells you the **line number** and what it expected. The most common beginner error is a missing semicolon: `error: expected ';'`.

**Your turn:** this program has two mistakes. Press **Check** first to see what the compiler says, then fix both so it prints `Fixed it` on one line.
hints: The compiler points at the line where it noticed the problem, which is sometimes the line *after* the real mistake.
Both `printf(...)` and `return 0` need a `;` at the end.

modules.title: Variables and types
modules.summary: Store values in named boxes. int, double and char, printing them with format specifiers, and constants.

steps.title: Your first variable
steps.text:
A **variable** is a named box that holds a value. In C you must say what *type* of value goes in the box.

```c
int kills = 25;
```

This creates a box named `kills` that holds an `int` (a whole number) and puts `25` in it.

To print it, `printf` needs a **format specifier** where the value should go. For an `int` that's `%d`:

```c
printf("Kills: %d\n", kills);
```

**Your turn:** declare an `int` named `score` with the value `42`.
hints: The type for whole numbers is `int`.

steps.title: Printing values with %d
steps.text:
`printf` replaces each `%d` with the next value after the format string, in order.

```c
int a = 3, b = 4;
printf("%d + %d\n", a, b);   // prints 3 + 4
```

**Your turn:** complete the `printf` so it prints `K/D: 20/5`.
hints: Put a `%d` for each number, then list the variables after the string in the same order.

steps.title: Changing a variable
steps.text:
A variable can be given a new value with `=`. The old value is replaced.

```c
int hp = 100;
hp = hp - 27;     // now 73
```

Read `hp = hp - 27` as: take the current value of `hp`, subtract 27, and store the result back in `hp`.

**Your turn:** the player has `3200` money and buys a rifle for `2700`. Subtract the price from `money` so the program prints `Money left: 500`.
hints: Write `money = money - 2700;` on the empty line.

require.message: Change `money` itself by subtracting 2700 from it (don't just print 500).

steps.title: Decimals with double
steps.text:
`int` can't hold fractions. For numbers with a decimal point use `double`, and print it with `%f`.

```c
double accuracy = 0.625;
printf("%f\n", accuracy);    // 0.625000
printf("%.2f\n", accuracy);  // 0.63 (rounded to 2 places)
```

`%.2f` means "two digits after the decimal point".

**Your turn:** store `1.25` in a `double` named `rating` and print it with exactly two decimals so the output is `Rating: 1.25`.
hints: The type is `double`. The format for two decimals is `%.2f`.

steps.title: Characters with char
steps.text:
A `char` holds a single character, written in **single** quotes: `'A'`. Double quotes make a string, which is a different thing.

Print a `char` with `%c`:

```c
char grade = 'B';
printf("Grade: %c\n", grade);
```

Under the hood a `char` is a small number (its ASCII code), so `'A'` is 65. Printing a char with `%d` shows that number.

**Your turn:** write a program that stores the letter `T` in a `char` named `team`, then prints two lines:

```
Team: T
Code: 84
```
hints: `char team = 'T';` declares it.
Use `%c` for the letter and `%d` for its number code.

require.message: Declare a variable named `team` of type `char`.

steps.title: Constants and sizeof
steps.text:
Put `const` in front of a declaration to make a variable read-only. Trying to change it later is a compile error, which protects you from accidents.

```c
const int MAX_PLAYERS = 10;
```

`sizeof` tells you how many bytes a type uses. On this site (and most machines) `int` is 4 bytes, `double` is 8 and `char` is always 1. Print a size with `%zu`.

**Your turn:** declare a constant `int` named `ROUND_TIME` equal to `115`, and print:

```
Round time: 115
int bytes: 4
```
hints: The keyword that makes a variable read-only is `const`.
`sizeof(int)` gives the size of an int in bytes.

modules.title: Operators and math
modules.summary: Arithmetic, the integer-division trap, the % remainder operator, precedence, shorthand operators and casts.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.text:
C has the usual math operators: `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide).

```c
int total = 12 * 3 + 4;   // 40
```

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just like in school math. Parentheses change the order: `12 * (3 + 4)` is 84.

**Your turn:** make the program print `Damage: 96` by filling in the operators. Base damage is 30, the multiplier is 4, armor absorbs 24.
hints: 30 times 4 is 120, and 120 minus 24 is 96.

steps.title: The integer division trap
steps.text:
When **both** sides of `/` are `int`, C does integer division: the fraction is thrown away (not rounded).

```c
printf("%d\n", 7 / 2);      // 3, not 3.5
printf("%f\n", 7.0 / 2);    // 3.500000
```

If either side is a `double`, you get a real division.

**Your turn:** 25 kills over 10 rounds should print `Kills per round: 2.50`. Right now it prints `2.00`. Fix the calculation of `kpr` so it does a real division.
hints: `kills / rounds` is computed as int / int (giving 2) *before* it's stored in the double.
Turn one side into a double first. Write `(double)kills / rounds`. That `(double)` is called a *cast*.

steps.title: Remainder with %
steps.text:
`%` (modulo) gives the **remainder** of an integer division.

```c
17 / 5   // 3
17 % 5   // 2   (17 = 3*5 + 2)
```

It's great for "is this even?" (`n % 2 == 0`) and for splitting units.

**Your turn:** a match lasted `754` seconds. Print it as minutes and seconds: `12 min 34 sec`.
hints: Minutes are how many whole 60s fit into total, so `total / 60`.
Seconds are what's left over, so `total % 60`.

require.message: Use the `%` operator on `total` to get the seconds.

steps.title: Shorthand operators
steps.text:
Updating a variable with itself is so common that C has shortcuts:

| Shorthand | Means |
|---|---|
| `x += 5;` | `x = x + 5;` |
| `x -= 5;` | `x = x - 5;` |
| `x *= 2;` | `x = x * 2;` |
| `x++;` | `x = x + 1;` |
| `x--;` | `x = x - 1;` |

**Your turn:** fill in the shorthand operators so the program prints `Streak: 12`.
hints: The comments say what each line should do: add 1, double, add 1, subtract 1.

steps.title: Prefix vs postfix ++
steps.text:
`x++` and `++x` both add 1 to `x`, but they differ when used inside a bigger expression:

- `x++` (postfix) gives the **old** value, then increments.
- `++x` (prefix) increments first, then gives the **new** value.

```c
int a = 5;
int b = a++;   // b = 5, a = 6
int c = ++a;   // a = 7, c = 7
```

**Your turn:** make the program print `5 7 7` by choosing prefix or postfix for each blank. The variable `a` starts at 5.
hints: `b` must get the old value 5, so use postfix: `a++`. After that, `a` is 6.
`c` must be 7 and `a` must also be 7, so increment first: `++a`.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text:
Time to write a small calculation on your own.

A player's **ADR** (average damage per round) is total damage divided by rounds played. Given the variables below, print:

```

ADR: 83.60
```

Total damage is the sum of the three halves' damage (it's a long match: first half, second half, overtime).
hints: Add the three variables into an `int total`.
Watch out for integer division: `(double)total / rounds`.
Print with `%d` for the total and `%.2f` for the ADR.

modules.title: Reading input
modules.summary: Make programs interactive with scanf. Reading numbers, characters and words, and checking that the read worked.

steps.title: Read a number
steps.text:
`scanf` is the mirror image of `printf`: it reads values from input (stdin) into variables.

```c
int n;
scanf("%d", &n);
```

The `&` means "the address of `n`". scanf needs to know *where* to store the value, not what's currently in it. Forgetting `&` is the #1 scanf bug.

On this site, each test feeds the program some input. Use **Run with my input** to try your own.

**Your turn:** read an int and print it doubled. Input `21` prints `42`.
hints: scanf needs the address of the variable, written `&n`.

steps.title: Several values at once
steps.text:
One `scanf` can read several values. Whitespace (spaces, newlines) between them is skipped automatically for numbers.

```c
int a, b;
scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);
```

**Your turn:** read a player's kills and deaths and print their difference.

Input: `18 11` prints `+/-: 7`
hints: `scanf("%d %d", &kills, &deaths);`

steps.title: Reading doubles
hints: Read with `scanf("%lf", &c);`
Compute `double f = c * 9 / 5 + 32;` then print with `%.1f`.

steps.title: Characters and words
steps.text:
- `%c` reads **one character**, and it does *not* skip whitespace. Write `" %c"` (with a leading space) to skip spaces and newlines first.
- `%s` reads a **word** (up to the next space) into a char array. Arrays don't need `&`. You'll learn why in the pointers module.

```c
char name[32];
scanf("%31s", name);   // 31 = max chars, leaving room for the terminator
```

**Your turn:** the input is a name followed by a team letter, like `s1mple T`. Print `s1mple plays on T`.
hints: The format for one char is `%c`. The space before it in the format string skips the space in the input.
team is a plain char variable, so scanf needs its address, `&team`.

steps.title: Did the read work?

steps.title: And, or, not
steps.text:
Combine conditions with logical operators:

- `&&` (and): true only if **both** sides are true
- `||` (or): true if **at least one** side is true
- `!` (not): flips true and false

```c
if (money >= 2700 && !has_rifle) { ... }
```

In C, any non-zero number counts as true and `0` is false.

steps.text:
A year is a leap year if:

- it's divisible by 4, **and**
- it's **not** divisible by 100, **unless** it's also divisible by 400.

So 2024 and 2000 are leap years, but 1900 and 2023 are not.

steps.title: Scope and pass by value
steps.text:
Variables declared inside a function only exist inside it (**local scope**).

C passes arguments **by value**: the function gets a *copy*. Changing the parameter doesn't change the caller's variable:

```c
void reset(int hp) { hp = 100; }   // changes the copy only

int hp = 20;
reset(hp);
printf("%d\n", hp);   // still 20
```

(To change the caller's variable you need pointers, coming soon.)

steps.title: Recursion
steps.text:
A function can call itself. That's **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case** that stops, and a step that moves toward it.

```c
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;          // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);   // smaller problem
}
```

steps.title: Declare and index
steps.text:
An **array** is a fixed-size row of values of the same type, stored next to each other in memory.

```c
int ammo[3] = {30, 20, 7};
printf("%d\n", ammo[0]);   // 30, indexes start at 0
```

modules.title: Strings
modules.summary: C strings are char arrays ending in '\0'. Length, copying, comparing, and writing string functions yourself.

steps.title: The null terminator
steps.text:
C has no built-in string type. A string is a **char array** that ends with the special character `'\0'` (value 0), called the **null terminator**.

```c
char name[] = "dust";
// stored as: 'd' 'u' 's' 't' '\0'   (5 chars!)
```

Functions like `printf("%s")` print characters until they hit `'\0'`. Forget it, and they keep reading random memory.

**Your turn:** build the string `"ak"` by hand and print it.
hints: The terminator character is written `'\0'` (backslash zero, in single quotes).

steps.text:

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `strlen(s)` | number of chars before `'\0'` |
| `strcpy(dst, src)` | copy src into dst |
| `strcat(dst, src)` | append src to dst |
| `strcmp(a, b)` | 0 if equal, negative/positive otherwise |

`dst` must be big enough, including room for the `'\0'`.

modules.title: Pointers
modules.summary: Addresses and the variables that hold them. & and *, changing a caller's variables, pointer arithmetic, arrays vs pointers, NULL and const.

steps.title: Addresses and pointers
steps.text:
Every variable lives at an **address** in memory. `&x` gives you that address. A **pointer** is a variable that stores an address.

```c
int hp = 100;
int *p = &hp;     // p points at hp
printf("%d\n", *p);   // 100: *p means "the value p points at"
*p = 75;              // changes hp itself!
printf("%d\n", hp);   // 75
```

- `int *p` declares "p is a pointer to int".
- `&hp` is "address of hp".
- `*p` (the **dereference** operator) is "the thing at that address".

**Your turn:** make `p` point at `armor`, then use `p` (not `armor` directly) to set it to `50`.
hints: The address of armor is `&armor`.
To write to the variable p points at, use `*p = ...`.

steps.title: Pointer arithmetic and arrays
steps.text:
An array's name turns into a pointer to its first element when you use it ("decays"). Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the **next element** (not the next byte):

```c
int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};
int *p = a;          // same as &a[0]
printf("%d\n", *(p + 1));   // 20
```

In fact `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. That's why arrays passed to functions can be modified: the function receives a pointer to the original elements.

steps.title: const and pointers
steps.text:
`const` can protect two different things, depending on where you put it:

| Declaration | Can change `*p`? | Can re-point `p`? |
|---|---|---|
| `const int *p` | no | yes |
| `int *const p` | yes | no |
| `const int *const p` | no | no |

Read it right to left: `const int *p` is "p is a pointer to an int that is const".

Professional C code marks every pointer parameter it only reads as `const int *`. It documents the promise ("I won't change your data") and the compiler enforces it.

A function can also **return** a pointer into the caller's array. If the array was `const`, the returned pointer must be `const` too.

```
"a b  c"      read ->  a _ b _ _ c
```

modules.title: Dynamic memory
modules.summary: The stack vs the heap. malloc, free, calloc and realloc, growing arrays, and who owns what.

steps.title: Stack vs heap
steps.text:
So far every variable lived on the **stack**: it's created when its block starts and destroyed automatically when the block ends. Stack arrays need a size known up front, and they die when the function returns.

The **heap** is memory you request at runtime and give back when you're done:

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));   // room for n ints
if (a == NULL) { /* out of memory */ }
a[0] = 42;                          // use it like an array
free(a);                            // give it back
```

`malloc` returns `NULL` if it fails. Every `malloc` needs exactly one matching `free`.

**Your turn:** allocate room for `n` ints.
hints: `malloc(bytes)` allocates; the number of bytes is `n * sizeof(int)`.
The function that releases heap memory is `free`.

steps.title: Size decided at runtime
steps.text:
The real power of `malloc`: the size can come from input.

**Your turn:** read `n`, then `n` numbers into a heap array. Print how many are **above the average**. Free the array at the end.

Input `4` / `2 4 6 8` (average 5) prints `2`.
hints: `int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));`
Two passes. The first reads and sums, the second counts values greater than the average.
Compare with a double average: `a[i] > (double)sum / n`.

require.message: Allocate the array with `malloc` (the size comes from input).
Don't forget to `free` the array.

steps.title: Return heap memory from a function

steps.title: calloc and strdup-style copies
steps.text:
- `calloc(count, size)` allocates **and zeroes** the memory.
- To keep a copy of a string, allocate `strlen(s) + 1` bytes (the +1 is for `'\0'`) and copy it in.

**Your turn:** write `char *copy_string(const char *s)` that returns a new heap copy of `s`.
hints: Allocate `strlen(s) + 1` bytes.
Copy with `strcpy(c, s)` (or memcpy of n + 1 bytes) and return c.

hints: Before storing, check `if (count == cap)`. If so, double cap and realloc.
`a[count++] = x;` stores and advances in one go.

steps.title: Memory bugs to avoid
steps.text:
The classic heap mistakes, which C won't catch for you:

| Bug | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Leak** | forgetting `free`; memory is lost until the program exits |
| **Use after free** | using a pointer after `free`; it may point at reused memory |
| **Double free** | freeing twice; corrupts the allocator |
| **Out of bounds** | writing past the end; silently corrupts neighbours |

A good habit: set a pointer to `NULL` right after freeing it. `free(NULL)` is safe and does nothing.

**Your turn:** this function should build a message but it has two memory bugs (a missing `+ 1` for the terminator, and a leak of `tmp`). Fix both so it returns `"gg wp"` correctly.
hints: "gg wp" needs 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 chars **plus** the terminator. Add `+ 1` to the size of `out`.
`tmp` is only a scratch copy. Call `free(tmp);` before returning.

require.message: `tmp` is never freed. That's a leak.
The size for `out` has no room for the `'\0'` terminator. Add `+ 1`.

steps.title: A 2D grid on the heap
steps.text:
When a grid's size is only known at runtime, a common layout is an **array of row pointers**, each row its own allocation:

```
grid ──> [ row0 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
         [ row1 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
         [ row2 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
```

```c
int **g = malloc(rows * sizeof *g);        // the row pointers
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    g[r] = calloc(cols, sizeof *g[r]);     // each row, zeroed
```

`sizeof *g` means "the size of whatever g points at". It stays correct even if you change the type later, which is why many style guides prefer it.

Freeing goes in reverse: every row first, then the array of pointers. If any allocation fails halfway, free what you already allocated and return `NULL`.

**Your turn:** write `make_grid` (all cells zero) and `free_grid`.
hints: First `int **g = malloc(rows * sizeof *g);`, then a loop with `g[r] = calloc(cols, sizeof *g[r]);`.
free_grid: `free(g[r])` for every row, then `free(g)`. Return early if g is NULL.

require.message: After freeing each row, free the array of row pointers too: `free(g);`

steps.title: Who owns what
steps.text:
C has no garbage collector, so every heap pointer needs an **owner**: the one piece of code responsible for freeing it. Professional C code writes this down in a comment next to each function:

```c
/* Returns a new array of new strings. The caller owns both:
   free each word, then the array, or call free_words(). */
char **split_words(const char *s, int *count);
```

A function that allocates something nested usually ships a matching "free" function, so callers can't get the order wrong.

**Your turn:** write `split_words`. It splits `s` on single spaces into separately allocated strings, stores how many in `*count`, and returns the array. Then write `free_words`. You can assume words are separated by exactly one space and `s` has no leading or trailing spaces. An empty string has 0 words (you may return `NULL` then).
hints: First count the words: one more than the number of spaces (unless the string is empty).
Allocate `n` pointers, then for each word allocate `len + 1` bytes, `memcpy` the letters and add `'\0'`.
`strchr(start, ' ')` finds the next space, or returns NULL for the last word.
free_words frees every word, then the array. `free(NULL)` is safe, so the empty case needs nothing special.

steps.title: Challenge: a string builder
steps.text:
Building a long string with repeated `strcat` into a fixed buffer is how buffer overflows happen. Real C code uses a **string builder**: a struct that owns a growing heap buffer.

```c
typedef struct {
    char *buf;   /* always '\0'-terminated once initialized */
    size_t len;  /* characters used, not counting '\0' */
    size_t cap;  /* bytes allocated */
} Builder;
```

**Your turn:** write the four functions:

- `sb_init(b)`: allocate a small starting buffer (say 8 bytes) holding `""`. Return 0 on success, -1 if allocation fails.
- `sb_append(b, s)`: append `s`, doubling `cap` as many times as needed. Return 0, or -1 if `realloc` fails (leave `b` unchanged then).
- `sb_str(b)`: return the current string.
- `sb_free(b)`: free the buffer and reset the fields.
hints: sb_init: set cap to 8, len to 0, `malloc` the buffer and put `'\0'` in it.
sb_append: you need `len + strlen(s) + 1` bytes. Double a local copy of cap until it's enough, then `realloc` into a temp pointer.
Copy with `memcpy(b->buf + b->len, s, add + 1)` so the terminator comes along, then add to len.

Real lists allocate nodes on the heap. Adding at the front is the easiest operation: the new node points at the old head, and becomes the new head.

The function has to change the caller's head pointer, so it takes a **pointer to the head pointer**:

modules.summary: Work with individual bits using bitwise operators and flags, and control compilation with #define and macros.

steps.title: #define constants
steps.text:
Lines starting with `#` are handled by the **preprocessor** before compilation. `#define` does a text substitution:

```c
#define MAX_ROUNDS 24
```

Every `MAX_ROUNDS` in the code is replaced with `24` before the compiler sees it. By convention macro names are UPPERCASE.

**Your turn:** define `TEAM_SIZE` as `5` so the program prints `10 players`.
hints: `#define NAME value`, with no `=` and no semicolon.

steps.title: Macro pitfalls
steps.text:
Macros can take arguments, but they're pure text replacement, which bites:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
SQUARE(1 + 2)   // becomes 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5, not 9!
```

The fix: wrap every argument **and** the whole body in parentheses:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
```

**Your turn:** `DOUBLE(3 + 4) * 2` should be 28, but this prints 18. Fix the `DOUBLE` macro.
hints: Expand it by hand: `3 + 4 + 3 + 4 * 2` = 18. The `* 2` only grabbed the last 4.
Wrap the argument and the body: `#define DOUBLE(x) ((x) + (x))`.

require.message: Parenthesize the macro fully: `((x) + (x))`.

steps.title: Bitwise operators
steps.text:
Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integers:

| Op | Name | Example (binary) |
|---|---|---|
| `&` | AND | `1100 & 1010 = 1000` |
| `\|` | OR | `1100 \| 1010 = 1110` |
| `^` | XOR | `1100 ^ 1010 = 0110` |
| `~` | NOT | flips every bit |
| `<<` | shift left | `0001 << 2 = 0100` |
| `>>` | shift right | `1000 >> 3 = 0001` |

`1 << n` is a number with only bit `n` set (that's 2 to the power n).

**Your turn:** write `int count_bits(unsigned x)` that returns how many bits are 1. Check the lowest bit with `x & 1`, then shift right.
steps.seed:
int count_bits(unsigned x) {

}
hints: Loop while x is not 0. Add `x & 1` to the count, then `x >>= 1`.

steps.title: Flags
steps.text:
Bits make compact on/off switches. Give each flag its own bit:

```c
#define HAS_HELMET  (1u << 0)
#define HAS_KIT     (1u << 1)
#define IS_SCOPED   (1u << 2)

unsigned state = 0;
state |= HAS_KIT;            // turn on
state &= ~HAS_KIT;           // turn off
state ^= IS_SCOPED;          // toggle
if (state & HAS_HELMET) {}   // test
```

**Your turn:** fill in the operators.

steps.title: Challenge: power of two
steps.text:
A classic bit trick: a positive number is a power of two exactly when it has a single 1 bit. And `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so for powers of two it gives 0.

**Your turn:** write `int is_pow2(unsigned x)` returning 1 or 0, without loops.

modules.title: Function pointers and callbacks
modules.summary: Treat functions as values. Function pointer syntax, typedefs, dispatch tables, qsort comparators, generic code with void*, and callbacks that carry context.

steps.title: Functions have addresses
steps.text:
A function lives in memory like everything else, so you can store its address in a **function pointer** and call it later:

```c
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

int (*op)(int, int) = add;   // op points at add
printf("%d\n", op(2, 3));    // 5
```

Read `int (*op)(int, int)` as: "op is a pointer to a function taking (int, int) and returning int". The parentheses around `*op` matter: without them, `int *op(int, int)` declares a *function* returning `int *`.

**Your turn:** point `op` at `sub` and call it.
hints: A function's name used as a value is its address: `op = sub;`
Call through the pointer exactly like a function: `op(10, 4)`.

steps.title: typedef and passing callbacks
steps.text:
Function pointer types get unreadable fast, so give them a name with `typedef`:

```c
typedef int (*BinOp)(int, int);
```

Now `BinOp` is a type, and you can pass behavior into a function. The function you pass is called a **callback**:

```c
int fold(const int *a, int n, int init, BinOp f);
fold(a, n, 0, add);   // sum
fold(a, n, 1, mul);   // product
```

**Your turn:** write `fold`. It starts with `init` and combines it with each element in order: `acc = f(acc, a[i])`.
hints: `int acc = init;` then for each element `acc = f(acc, a[i]);`

```c

```

That's how GUI toolkits, `pthread_create`, network libraries and game engines all do callbacks in C.

modules.title: Integer types and undefined behavior
modules.summary: How big each integer type really is, unsigned wraparound, signed overflow, fixed-width types, size_t traps, floating-point rounding, and the undefined behavior every C programmer must recognize.

steps.title: Sizes and limits
steps.text:
C only promises **minimum** sizes. On today's common platforms:

| Type | Usual size | Range (signed) |
|---|---|---|
| `char` | 1 byte | -128 to 127 |
| `short` | 2 bytes | about ±32 thousand |
| `int` | 4 bytes | about ±2.1 billion |
| `long` | 4 **or** 8 bytes | depends on the platform! |
| `long long` | 8 bytes | about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ |

`long` is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux and macOS, but 4 bytes on Windows and on 32-bit systems (including the WebAssembly this site runs on). Code that assumes one or the other breaks when it moves. That's why professional code uses the exact-width types you'll meet in a few steps.

`<limits.h>` gives the real limits for the platform you compile on: `INT_MAX`, `INT_MIN`, `LLONG_MAX`, `UINT_MAX`, `CHAR_BIT` (bits in a byte, 8 everywhere you'll ever work).

**Your turn:** print the largest `int`, then the smallest.
hints: The macros are `INT_MAX` and `INT_MIN`, from `<limits.h>`.

steps.title: Unsigned wraparound
steps.text:
Unsigned integers can't be negative. Their arithmetic is defined to **wrap around** modulo 2ᴺ: go below 0 and you land at the top.

```c
unsigned int x = 0;
x = x - 1;               // 4294967295, not -1
```

This is well-defined (unlike signed overflow, next step), and it's useful for hashing and bit manipulation. It's also a classic trap in countdown loops:

```c
for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)   // i >= 0 is ALWAYS true: infinite loop
```

The idiomatic safe countdown tests *before* decrementing:

```c
for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )         // visits n-1, n-2, ..., 0
```

**Your turn:** read a count `n` and then `n` integers into an array (at most 100), and print them in **reverse** order on one line, separated by spaces. Use a `size_t` index for the reverse loop.
hints: `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )` checks i > 0 and *then* decrements, so the body sees n-1 down to 0.
Print a space after every number except the last one printed (when i is 0).

require.message: Count down with a `size_t` index, starting from `n`: `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )`.

steps.title: Signed overflow is undefined
steps.text:
For **signed** integers, going past `INT_MAX` is **undefined behavior** (UB). "Undefined" doesn't mean "wraps around". It means the C standard puts *no requirements at all* on what happens, and optimizers rely on that. For example, the compiler may delete `if (x + 1 < x)` entirely, because in a program without UB that condition can never be true.

So you must check **before** the operation, using only operations that can't overflow:

```c
if (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b)  /* a + b would overflow upward */
if (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b)  /* a + b would overflow downward */
```

(GCC and Clang also offer `__builtin_add_overflow`, and C23 standardizes `ckd_add` in `<stdckdint.h>`. It's still worth knowing how to write the check yourself.)

**Your turn:** write `int checked_add(int a, int b, int *out)`. If the sum fits, store it in `*out` and return 1. Otherwise return 0 and leave `*out` untouched.
hints: Positive b: the sum overflows exactly when `a > INT_MAX - b`. That subtraction is safe because b > 0.
Negative b: the sum underflows exactly when `a < INT_MIN - b`.
Only compute `a + b` after both checks pass.

forbid.message: Write the check with plain `int` comparisons against INT_MAX and INT_MIN.

steps.title: Fixed-width types
steps.text:
`<stdint.h>` gives types with an **exact** size on every platform:

| Type | Size | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `int8_t` / `uint8_t` | 1 byte | raw bytes, pixels |
| `int32_t` / `uint32_t` | 4 bytes | file formats, protocols |
| `int64_t` / `uint64_t` | 8 bytes | big counters, hashes, timestamps |

Whenever data leaves the program (files, network packets, hashes), professional code uses these instead of `int` or `long`, so it means the same thing on every machine.

To print them portably, `<inttypes.h>` has format macros: `printf("%" PRIu64 "\n", x);`

**Your turn:** implement the 64-bit **FNV-1a** hash, a simple, widely used string hash:

```
hash = 14695981039346656037
for each byte b of the string:
    hash = hash XOR b
    hash = hash * 1099511628211      (wrapping, which uint64_t does for free)
```
hints: Start with `uint64_t h = 14695981039346656037ULL;`. The `ULL` suffix makes the constant unsigned long long.
Walk the string as `unsigned char` so bytes above 127 aren't negative: `(const unsigned char *)s`.

steps.title: The signed/unsigned comparison trap
steps.text:
When you compare a signed `int` with an unsigned value like `size_t` (what `strlen` and `sizeof` return), C converts the **int to unsigned** first. A negative int becomes a huge positive number:

```c
int n = -1;
if (strlen("abc") > n)   // false! -1 becomes 18446744073709551615 (or 4294967295)
```

`-Wall -Wextra` warns about this (`-Wsign-compare`). Treat that warning as a bug report, not noise.

**Your turn:** `longer_than(s, n)` should return 1 when `s` has more than `n` characters. It's wrong for negative `n` (every string is longer than -1 characters). Fix it without casting the length to `int` (strings can be longer than `INT_MAX`).

steps.title: Floating-point rounding
steps.text:
`double` stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions (like 0.1) have no exact binary form. So:

```c
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3    // false! 0.30000000000000004 vs 0.29999999999999998
```

Two rules professionals follow:

1. **Never compare doubles with `==`** after arithmetic. Check they're *close enough*, relative to their size.
2. **Never store money in `double`.** Store integer **cents** (`int64_t`), and only format as dollars for display.

A good closeness test scales the tolerance with the numbers:

```
|a - b| <= eps * max(1, |a|, |b|)
```

**Your turn:** write `int nearly_equal(double a, double b, double eps)` using that formula. Don't use `<math.h>`; write the absolute value yourself.

steps.title: Challenge: hunt the undefined behavior
steps.text:
Undefined behavior is the biggest source of security holes in C. Learn to spot the usual suspects:

| UB | Example |
|---|---|
| Out-of-bounds access | `a[n]` in an array of n elements |
| Signed overflow | `INT_MAX + 1` |
| Reading uninitialized memory | `int x; printf("%d", x);` |
| Null or dangling pointer use | `*NULL`, use after `free` |
| Shifting too far | `1 << 32` on a 32-bit int |
| Modifying twice without sequencing | `i = i++ + 1;` |

The worst part: UB often *seems* to work, until a new compiler version, an optimization level or an input changes. On a real machine, `-fsanitize=address,undefined` catches most of these at runtime (the Pro Track covers it).

**Your turn:** these two functions each have undefined behavior. Fix both:

- `sum` reads one element past the end of the array.
- `midpoint` overflows for large inputs. Compute it without overflowing (assume `lo <= hi`).
hints: An array of n elements has indexes 0 to n - 1. The loop condition should be `i < n`.
`lo + (hi - lo) / 2` never overflows when lo <= hi, because `hi - lo` fits.

steps.title: References are aliases
steps.text:
A **reference** is another name for an existing variable. Declare one with `&` after the type:

```cpp
int hp = 100;
int& ref = hp;   // ref IS hp
ref -= 30;       // hp is now 70
```

Unlike pointers, a reference must be initialized, can't be null, and can't be re-pointed later. No `*` or `->` needed to use it.

**Your turn:** make `alias` a reference to `money`, then spend 800 through it.

steps.title: Pass by reference
steps.text:

```cpp
void heal(int& hp) { hp = 100; }

int hp = 12;
heal(hp);        // no & at the call site
```

steps.title: const references
steps.text:
Passing a `std::string` or a big object by value **copies** it. Passing by reference avoids the copy, and adding `const` promises you won't modify it. This is the everyday C++ way to take read-only parameters:

```cpp
int count_spaces(const std::string& s);
```

Rule of thumb: small types (`int`, `double`, `char`) by value, everything bigger by `const&`.

steps.title: Member initializer lists
steps.text:
A constructor's **initializer list** (after the `:`) builds each member directly. Assigning inside the body instead first default-constructs the member and then overwrites it.

```cpp
Player(std::string name, int hp) : name_(std::move(name)), hp_(hp) {}
```

Some members *must* be set in the initializer list, because they can't be assigned later:

- `const` members
- reference members
- members whose type has no default constructor

Members are always initialized in the order they are **declared in the class**, not the order you list them. `-Wall` warns when the two orders differ (`-Wreorder`), because reading a member that isn't built yet is a real bug.

**Your turn:** give `Player` a constructor `Player(const std::string& name, int max_hp)` that sets the const `name_`, sets `max_hp_`, and starts `hp_` at `max_hp_`. Use the initializer list for all three.

List members in the same order they are declared: name_, max_hp_, hp_. Then `hp_(max_hp_)` is safe because max_hp_ is already built.

steps.title: Keeping invariants
steps.text:
An **invariant** is a rule that must be true for every object, at all times, from the outside. For a health bar: `0 <= hp <= max`.

This is the real reason for `private`: if only member functions can touch the data, only they can break the rule, and you check it in one place. Every constructor must *establish* the invariant and every member function must *preserve* it.

```cpp
void damage(int amount) {
    hp_ = std::max(0, hp_ - amount);   // never below 0
}
```

**Your turn:** write class `Health`:

- `Health(int max)`: max below 1 becomes 1; starts full
- `void damage(int n)` and `void heal(int n)`: negative amounts are ignored; hp stays within `0..max`
- `int hp() const`, `int max() const`, `bool alive() const`
hints: Constructor: `explicit Health(int max) : max_(std::max(1, max)), hp_(max_) {}`
`damage`: if n > 0, `hp_ = std::max(0, hp_ - n);`. `heal` is the mirror image with `std::min(max_, ...)`.

- `int num() const`, `int den() const`
- `Fraction plus(const Fraction& o) const` and `Fraction times(const Fraction& o) const`

`std::gcd(a, b)` from `<numeric>` gives the greatest common divisor (it handles negative numbers).

`gcd(0, d)` is `d`, so 0/5 becomes 0/1 automatically.
`plus` and `times` just build a new Fraction and let the constructor reduce it: a/b + c/d = (ad + cb) / bd.

steps.title: Copy assignment with copy-and-swap
steps.text:
Copy **assignment** (`a = b;` on an existing `a`) is harder than the copy constructor: `a` already owns memory that must be released, and `a = a;` must not destroy itself.

The standard trick is **copy-and-swap**:

```cpp
void swap(IntArray& other) noexcept {
    std::swap(data_, other.data_);
    std::swap(n_, other.n_);
}
IntArray& operator=(IntArray other) {   // by value: a copy is made here
    swap(other);                        // take the copy's guts
    return *this;                       // other's destructor frees our old data
}
```

Why professionals like it:

- It reuses the copy constructor, so there's no duplicated copying code.
- Self-assignment is automatically safe.
- If the copy throws (runs out of memory), `*this` is untouched. That's called the **strong exception guarantee**.

**Your turn:** write the member `swap` and the copy-and-swap `operator=`.

steps.title: Challenge: a scope guard

RAII isn't only for memory. Any "undo" action (close a file, unlock a mutex, roll back a transaction, restore a setting) can be tied to a destructor, so it runs however the scope is left: normal end, early `return`, or an exception.

A **scope guard** holds a function and calls it in its destructor, unless you `dismiss()` it first (for example, because the operation succeeded and there's nothing to undo). Many large codebases have one; C++ proposals call it `scope_exit`.

`std::function<void()>` can hold any callable that takes no arguments, including a lambda.

**Your turn:** write class `ScopeGuard`:

- `explicit ScopeGuard(std::function<void()> f)`
- the destructor calls `f` unless dismissed
- `void dismiss()`
- it must not be copyable (two copies would run the action twice)

```cpp
auto square = [](int x) { return x * x; };
square(5);   // 25
```

- `(int x)` are the parameters
- the return type is deduced

steps.title: Captures

A lambda can use variables from the surrounding scope if it **captures** them:

| Capture | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[x]` | copy of x |
| `[&x]` | reference to x |
| `[=]` | copy everything used |
| `[&]` | reference everything used |

```cpp
int limit = 50;
auto big = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [limit](int x) { return x > limit; });

int total = 0;
std::for_each(v.begin(), v.end(), [&total](int x) { total += x; });
```

steps.title: unique_ptr
steps.text:
`std::unique_ptr<T>` (from `<memory>`) owns one heap object and deletes it automatically when the unique_ptr goes away. It's RAII for heap memory, and it costs nothing extra at runtime.

```cpp
auto p = std::make_unique<Player>("ropz", 100);
p->take_damage(30);     // use it like a pointer
// no delete needed, ever
```

steps.title: Unique means unique
steps.text:
A `unique_ptr` can't be **copied** (two owners would both delete). It can be **moved**, which transfers ownership and leaves the source empty (null):

```cpp
auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5);
// auto b = a;               // compile error: copying is deleted
auto b = std::move(a);       // ok: b owns it, a is now nullptr
```

Functions that take ownership accept `std::unique_ptr<T>` by value; callers must `std::move` into them.

**Your turn:** complete `Inventory::add`, which takes ownership of an item and stores it in the vector. Then `count()` and `total_value()`.

steps.title: shared_ptr
steps.text:
`std::shared_ptr<T>` allows **several owners**. It keeps a reference count and deletes the object when the last owner goes away. `use_count()` shows how many owners there are.

```cpp
auto a = std::make_shared<int>(7);   // count 1
auto b = a;                          // copying is fine: count 2
```

Prefer `unique_ptr` by default. Reach for `shared_ptr` only when ownership is genuinely shared.

modules.title: Move semantics
modules.summary: Why C++ can pass big objects around cheaply. lvalues vs rvalues, std::move, move constructors and the rule of five.

steps.title: Copies are expensive
steps.text:
Copying a `std::vector` with a million elements copies a million elements. But often the source is about to disappear anyway (a temporary, or a variable you're done with). In that case you can **steal** its internals instead: that's a **move**.

- An **lvalue** is something with a name that lives on (`v`).
- An **rvalue** is a temporary about to die (`make_vector()`, `a + b`).

`std::move(x)` doesn't move anything by itself. It *casts* `x` to an rvalue, which says "I'm done with x, you may steal from it".

After a move, the source is in a valid but unspecified state. Don't read its value; you may assign a new one.

**Your turn:** move `big` into `store` instead of copying it.
hints: Wrap it: `std::move(big)`.

hints: Signature: `Buffer(Buffer&& other) noexcept`.

hints: Signature: `Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& other) noexcept`.

steps.title: Return by value is free
steps.text:
Returning a local object by value doesn't copy it. When you return a temporary (`return Widget(...);`), C++17 **guarantees** the object is built directly in the caller's variable: no copy, no move. Returning a named local is almost always optimized the same way, and otherwise it's moved.

So write functions that return by value; don't return pointers or use out-parameters for performance.

**Your turn:** the `Tracker` struct counts copies. Write `Tracker make_tracker(int id)` so that creating one via your function performs **zero** copies. The test prints the copy count.
hints: Just `return Tracker(id);`. Guaranteed copy elision does the rest.

steps.title: Moved-from objects
steps.text:
After `b = std::move(a);`, what is `a`? For standard library types the rule is **valid but unspecified**:

- You **may** destroy it, assign it a new value, or call functions with no preconditions (`clear()`, `empty()`, `size()`).
- You **must not** rely on its value. A moved-from `std::string` is usually empty, but nothing promises that.

So the professional habit is: after moving from something, either stop using it or reset it explicitly.

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> batch = std::move(pending);
pending.clear();   // now it's definitely empty and ready to reuse
```

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<std::string> take_all(std::vector<std::string>& src)` that moves the whole contents out of `src` (no element copies) and leaves `src` definitely empty.
hints: `std::vector<std::string> out = std::move(src);` steals src's buffer in one go.
Then `src.clear();` so the caller gets a known state, and `return out;`.

steps.title: Sink parameters and emplace_back
steps.text:
When a function is going to **keep** a string (store it in a member or a container), take it **by value** and move it into place. This is called a *sink* parameter:

```cpp
explicit Player(std::string name) : name_(std::move(name)) {}
```

- Caller passes a temporary: it's moved in twice, zero copies.
- Caller passes a variable it still needs: exactly one copy, which is unavoidable.

For containers, `emplace_back(args...)` constructs the element **inside** the vector from constructor arguments, instead of building a temporary and moving it in.

```cpp
team.emplace_back("ropz");   // calls Player(std::string) in place
```

**Your turn:** give `Player` a sink constructor, and write `void recruit(std::vector<Player>& team, std::string name)` that adds a player using `emplace_back` and moves the name.

```cpp
return std::exchange(lines_, {});   // hand over the lines, leave an empty vector
```

steps.title: constexpr
steps.text:
`constexpr` functions can run **at compile time** when given constant inputs. The result is baked into the program:

```cpp
constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }
static_assert(square(12) == 144);   // checked by the compiler!
int arr[square(3)];                 // array size known at compile time
```

steps.title: Values as template parameters
steps.text:
Template parameters don't have to be types. A **non-type template parameter** is a compile-time value, usually a size:

```cpp
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Ring { T items_[N]; /* ... */ };

Ring<int, 8> r;    // N is 8, baked in at compile time
```

That's exactly how `std::array<int, 5>` works. The size lives in the **type**, so there's no heap allocation, and `Ring<int, 8>` and `Ring<int, 16>` are different types.

**Your turn:** write `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class FixedStack` backed by a plain array `T items_[N]`:

steps.title: Template specialization
steps.text:
Sometimes one type needs different behavior from the general template. A **full specialization** provides a replacement for exactly that type:

```cpp
template <typename T>
struct TypeName { static std::string get() { return "unknown"; } };

template <>
struct TypeName<int> { static std::string get() { return "int"; } };
```

`template <>` with empty brackets means "all the parameters are already fixed". The compiler picks the most specific match. This is how the standard library implements things like `std::hash<std::string>`, and how you add support for your own types to library templates.

**Your turn:** add specializations of `TypeName` for `double` (`"double"`), `bool` (`"bool"`) and `std::string` (`"string"`).

- `void push(const T& v)`
- `void pop()` (assume non-empty)
- `const T& top() const`
- `const T& min() const`: the smallest element currently in the stack
- `bool empty() const`

Hint for the O(1) min: alongside each value, remember what the minimum was at that point. Or keep a second stack of minimums.

On push, also push onto `mins_` when the value is less than or equal to the current min.
On pop, if the value leaving equals `mins_.back()`, pop `mins_` too.

steps.text:
Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer only runs the **base** destructor. The derived part never gets cleaned up.

steps.title: Calling the base version, and protected
steps.text:
An override often wants to **extend** the base behavior, not replace it. Call the base version by naming it:

```cpp
std::string describe() const override {
    return Unit::describe() + " [elite]";
}
```

Access levels, one more time:

| Keyword | Who can use it |
|---|---|
| `public` | everyone |
| `protected` | the class **and classes derived from it** |
| `private` | only the class itself |

Use `protected` sparingly. Every protected member is part of the contract with all future subclasses, so it's as hard to change later as a public one.

**Your turn:** finish `Medic`. Its `describe()` returns the base description plus `" +heal"`, and `heal(Unit& u)` restores `u` by the protected `power_` amount (use `u.restore(...)`).

steps.title: Composition over inheritance
steps.text:
Inheritance means **is-a**: a `Pistol` *is a* `Weapon`. For **has-a** relationships, use a member instead. That's *composition*:

```cpp
class Squad : public std::vector<Player> { };   // wrong: a squad isn't a vector
class Squad { std::vector<Player> members_; };   // right: a squad has members
```

Why composition is the default in professional code:

- The class controls its own interface. Inheriting from `std::vector` would expose `erase`, `clear` and everything else, letting callers break your rules.
- You can swap the member's type later without touching callers.
- Standard containers have no virtual destructor, so they aren't meant to be base classes at all.

**Your turn:** write class `Squad` that *has* a `std::vector<std::string>` of names, with a maximum size of 5:

- `bool add(const std::string& name)`: false if full or already in the squad
- `bool remove(const std::string& name)`: false if not found
- `int size() const`, `std::string roster() const` (names joined with `", "`, in join order)

steps.title: Challenge: program to an interface
steps.text:
In enterprise code, the most valuable use of virtual functions isn't game units: it's **dependency injection**. A class depends on an abstract *interface* instead of a concrete service, and whoever creates it passes in the real thing.

```cpp
class Clock { public: virtual ~Clock() = default; virtual long now() const = 0; };
class Session { public: explicit Session(const Clock& c); /* uses c.now() */ };
```

Production code passes a clock that reads the system time. **Tests** pass a fake clock they control, so time-dependent logic can be tested instantly and reliably. The same idea covers databases, network clients and file systems.

**Your turn:** write `class RateLimiter` that takes a `const Clock&` and allows at most `limit` calls to `allow()` in any window of `window` seconds. `allow()` returns true and records the call if under the limit, otherwise false. A call at time `t` falls out of the window once `now() >= t + window`.

In `allow()`: read `t = clock_.now()`, pop calls from the front while `t >= front + window_`.

steps.title: std::variant and std::visit
steps.text:
`std::variant<A, B, C>` holds exactly **one** of several types, and knows which. It's a type-safe union.

```cpp
std::variant<int, std::string> v = 5;
v = "hello";                               // now holds a string
std::holds_alternative<std::string>(v);    // true
std::get<std::string>(v);                  // "hello"
```

`std::visit` calls a function with whatever is inside. A lambda with an `auto` parameter handles every type:

```cpp
std::visit([](const auto& x) { std::cout << x; }, v);
```

**Your turn:** an `Event` is either a `Kill{attacker, victim}`, a `Plant{site}` or a `RoundEnd{winner}`. Write `std::string describe(const Event& e)` returning `"A killed B"`, `"bomb planted at X"` or `"round to W"`. Use `std::holds_alternative`/`std::get`, or `std::get_if`.

steps.title: std::string_view
steps.text:
`std::string_view` is a lightweight, **non-owning** view of characters: a pointer plus a length. It accepts string literals, `std::string`s and substrings without copying anything, which makes it the modern choice for read-only string parameters.

```cpp
int count_upper(std::string_view s);
count_upper("AWP");            // no std::string is created
s.substr(1, 2);                // also a view, no copy
s.starts_with("de_");          // C++20
```

Danger: a view doesn't keep the text alive. Never return a view of a local string.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.text:
A plain template accepts any type and fails with a wall of errors deep inside if the type doesn't fit. **Concepts** (C++20) state the requirements up front:

```cpp
#include <concepts>

template <std::integral T>
T gcd(T a, T b) { ... }       // only integer types allowed

gcd(12, 18);    // ok
gcd(1.5, 2.0);  // clear error: double doesn't satisfy integral
```

You can write your own with `requires`:

```cpp
template <typename T>
concept HasSize = requires(T t) { t.size(); };
```

steps.title: Passing errors up

Real programs are layers: `main` calls `load_config`, which calls `parse_line`, which calls `parse_int`. When the bottom layer fails, each layer above has two honest choices:

1. **Handle it** (use a default, retry, skip the item), or
2. **Pass it up** unchanged, usually with an early `return`.

The one dishonest choice is swallowing it: returning a made-up value as if nothing went wrong. That's how bugs travel far from where they started.

```cpp
auto n = parse_int(part);
if (!n) return std::nullopt;   // pass it up
total += *n;
```

projects.title: Build your own dynamic array
projects.summary: Write the growable array every language hides from you. malloc, realloc doubling, insert, remove and shrink, all tested by hidden unit tests.

milestones.title: New, push, get, free
milestones.text:
You're writing a library, so there's no `main`: hidden tests call your functions.

- `vec_new()` returns an empty vector with **capacity 4** (allocate the storage).
- `vec_push(v, x)` appends `x`. When `size == cap`, **double** the capacity with `realloc` first.
- `vec_get(v, i)` returns element `i` (you can assume `i` is valid).
- `vec_free(v)` frees the storage and sets `data` to NULL, size and cap to 0.
hints: vec_new: set cap to 4, size to 0, and `data = malloc(cap * sizeof(int))`.
vec_push: if `v->size == v->cap`, double cap and `v->data = realloc(v->data, v->cap * sizeof(int));`
Then `v->data[v->size++] = x;`

milestones.title: Pop and remove
milestones.text:
Add:

- `int vec_pop(IntVec *v)` removes and returns the last element (assume non-empty)
- `int vec_remove(IntVec *v, int i)` removes element `i`, shifts everything after it one place left, and returns the removed value
hints: pop: `return v->data[--v->size];`
remove: save the value, then shift `data[k] = data[k + 1]` for k from i up to size - 2, and decrease size.

milestones.title: Insert
milestones.text: Add `void vec_insert(IntVec *v, int i, int x)` that inserts `x` **before** index `i` (0 to size; inserting at `size` appends). Grow first if full, then shift elements right, starting from the end.
hints: Grow the same way push does.
Shift from the back: `for (int k = v->size; k > i; k--) v->data[k] = v->data[k - 1];`

milestones.title: Reserve and shrink
milestones.text:
Finish the library with capacity control:

- `void vec_reserve(IntVec *v, int cap)` grows the capacity to at least `cap` (never shrinks)
- `void vec_shrink(IntVec *v)` reduces the capacity to exactly `size` (but at least 1)

Both use `realloc`.
hints: reserve: return early if `cap <= v->cap`.
shrink: the target capacity is size, or 1 when empty.

projects.summary: A Matrix class with operators for addition, scaling, multiplication, transpose, printing and a determinant.

milestones.title: Storage and access
milestones.text:
Store the elements in one `std::vector<double>` in **row-major** order: element `(r, c)` lives at index `r * cols + c`.

Implement:

- `Matrix(int rows, int cols)` creates a zero-filled matrix
- `int rows() const`, `int cols() const`
- `double& at(int r, int c)` and `double at(int r, int c) const`
hints: Initialize `data_(rows * cols, 0.0)` in the initializer list.
`return data_[r * cols_ + c];`

milestones.title: Add, compare, scale
milestones.text:
Add non-member operators:

- `Matrix operator+(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)` (same size assumed)
- `bool operator==(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)` (same size and all elements equal)
- `Matrix operator*(const Matrix& m, double k)` (scale every element)
hints: Build a result matrix of the same size and fill it with nested loops.
For ==, compare sizes first, then every element.

milestones.title: Matrix multiplication
milestones.text:
Add `Matrix operator*(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)`: an `n x m` times an `m x p` gives an `n x p` matrix where

```
out(r, c) = sum over k of a(r, k) * b(k, c)
```

Also add a static `Matrix::identity(int n)` returning the `n x n` identity matrix (1 on the diagonal).
hints: The result has a's rows and b's columns.
Three nested loops. The innermost sums `a.at(r, k) * b.at(k, c)`.
`static Matrix identity(int n)` goes inside the class.

milestones.title: Transpose and printing
milestones.text:
Add:

- `Matrix transpose() const` (rows become columns)
- `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&, const Matrix&)` that prints each row on its own line, elements separated by single spaces, e.g. `1 2 3`. Print numbers with plain `<<` (so 2.5 prints as `2.5` and 3.0 prints as `3`).
hints: transpose: result is cols x rows with `t.at(c, r) = at(r, c)`.
operator<<: a space before every element except the first in each row, then `'\n'`.

milestones.title: Determinant
milestones.text:
Add `double determinant() const` for square matrices. The recursive **cofactor expansion** along the first row is the easiest to write:

```
det([a]) = a
det(M) = sum over c of (-1)^c * M(0, c) * det(minor(0, c))
```

where `minor(0, c)` is M without row 0 and column c. (It's slow for big matrices, and that's fine here.)
hints: Base case 1x1 returns the element.
For each column c of row 0: build the minor by copying rows 1..n-1 and skipping column c.
Alternate the sign: + for even c, - for odd c.

projects.summary: Re-implement std::vector as a class template. Growth, deep copies, moves, iterators, so it works with range-for and std::sort.

milestones.title: Grow and index
milestones.text:
Build `Vec<T>` step by step. Storage is a raw array from `new T[cap]`, released with `delete[]`. (That requires `T` to be default-constructible. The real `std::vector` uses lower-level tricks to avoid that; you don't need them here.)

Implement:

- a default constructor (empty, no allocation) and a destructor
- `void push_back(const T& x)`: when full, grow capacity to `cap == 0 ? 1 : cap * 2`, allocate a new array, **move** the old elements across, delete the old array
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`
- `T& operator[](std::size_t i)` and a const version

For now, delete the copy operations (`Vec(const Vec&) = delete;` and the same for `operator=`) so nothing copies by accident.
hints: A private helper `void grow(std::size_t new_cap)` keeps push_back short.
In grow: `T* fresh = new T[new_cap];` move elements with `fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i]);`, then `delete[] data_; data_ = fresh;`.

milestones.title: Deep copies
hints: Copy constructor: allocate `new T[other.size_]` (or nullptr when empty) and copy element by element.
Copy assignment takes its parameter **by value**, then swaps. The parameter's destructor frees the old contents.

milestones.title: Moves
milestones.text:
Add a move constructor and a move assignment. They steal the pointer and leave the source empty (`nullptr`, size 0, capacity 0). Mark them `noexcept`.

Because copy assignment takes its parameter by value, the move assignment is optional (the by-value parameter can be move-constructed), but write the move constructor for sure.
hints: `Vec(Vec&& other) noexcept : data_(other.data_), size_(other.size_), cap_(other.cap_) { ...reset other... }`

milestones.title: Iterators, back and pop_back
milestones.text:
Make `Vec` work with range-for and the standard algorithms by adding iterators. For a contiguous array, plain pointers **are** iterators:

```cpp
T* begin() { return data_; }
T* end() { return data_ + size_; }
```

Add const versions too, plus `T& back()`, `void pop_back()` and `bool empty() const`.

Then `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` and `for (auto& x : v)` just work.
hints: `T* begin() { return data_; }` and `T* end() { return data_ + size_; }`, plus const overloads returning `const T*`.
`back()` is `data_[size_ - 1]`; `pop_back()` just decrements size_.

projects.title: Expression interpreter
projects.summary: A calculator language with precedence, parentheses, variables and error messages. Tokenizer, recursive-descent parser and evaluator, no exceptions.

milestones.title: Plus and minus
milestones.text:
Each input line is an expression of integers with `+` and `-`, spaces optional. Print its value.

```
1 + 2 - 3 + 10
100-1
42
```
prints
```
10
99
42
```

Walk the string with an index. Skip spaces, read a number digit by digit, then repeatedly read an operator and another number.
hints: A small struct holding the string and a position `i` keeps the parsing functions tidy.
`number()`: skip spaces, then `v = v * 10 + (s[i++] - '0')` while the char is a digit.
`expr()`: read a number, then loop: if the next char is + or -, consume it, read another number and combine.

milestones.title: Precedence
milestones.text:
Add `*` and `/` (integer division), which bind tighter than `+` and `-`. The classic **recursive descent** grammar:

```
expr   = term   { ("+" | "-") term }
term   = factor { ("*" | "/") factor }
factor = number
```

Each rule becomes a function that calls the next one down.

`2 + 3 * 4` prints `14`; `20 / 3 * 3` prints `18`.
hints: An `eat(char c)` helper that skips spaces and consumes c if it's next makes every rule shorter.
term() is just like expr() but with * and /, and it calls factor() instead of term().

milestones.title: Parentheses and unary minus
milestones.text:
Extend `factor`:

```
factor = number | "(" expr ")" | "-" factor
```

`(2 + 3) * 4` prints `20`; `-(4 - 10)` prints `6`; `--3` prints `3`.
hints: factor() now checks three cases: a `-` (negate the next factor), a `(` (parse a whole expr, then eat `)`), or a number.
Calling expr() from factor() is fine. That mutual recursion is what makes nesting work.

milestones.title: Variables
milestones.text:
Add variables stored in a `std::map<std::string, long long>` (or unordered_map):

- `let NAME = EXPR` stores the value and prints `NAME = VALUE`
- a name inside an expression is replaced by its value

Names are letters and underscores. The map must survive from line to line.

```
let hp = 100
let dmg = 27 * 2
hp - dmg
```
prints
```
hp = 100
dmg = 54
46
```
hints: Check whether the line starts with `let ` before parsing an expression.
In factor(): if the next char is a letter or `_`, read a name and return its value from the map.
The map lives outside the loop (a global or a variable in main passed to the parser).

projects.title: Write a memory allocator
projects.summary: See what malloc does underneath. A bump allocator with alignment, then a fixed-size pool allocator built on a free list.

milestones.title: Bump allocator
milestones.text:
The simplest allocator hands out memory from one big array by moving a pointer forward ("bumping" it). It can't free individual blocks, only reset everything at once. Game engines use exactly this for per-frame scratch memory.

- `void *bump_alloc(size_t n)` returns `heap + used` and advances `used` by `n`. If fewer than `n` bytes are left, return `NULL` and change nothing.
- `void bump_reset(void)` makes all 4096 bytes available again.
hints: Bytes left are `sizeof(heap) - used`. Compare with that (not `used + n > 4096`) to avoid overflow.
Return `heap + used` before advancing.

milestones.title: Alignment
milestones.text:
CPUs want an `int` at an address divisible by 4, a `double` by 8, and so on. `malloc` guarantees suitably aligned memory, so yours should too.

Round every request **up to a multiple of 8** before bumping, so every returned address is 8-aligned (the heap itself starts 16-aligned):

```c
size_t rounded = (n + 7) & ~(size_t)7;
```

Also make `bump_alloc(0)` return `NULL`.
hints: `(n + 7) & ~(size_t)7` clears the low 3 bits after adding 7, rounding up to a multiple of 8.
Use the rounded size for both the space check and the bump.

milestones.title: A pool with a free list
milestones.text:
A **pool allocator** hands out blocks of one fixed size, and *can* free them individually. The trick: free blocks store a pointer to the next free block **inside themselves**, forming a linked list that costs zero extra memory.

```c
#define BLOCK 16
#define BLOCKS 32
static _Alignas(16) unsigned char pool[BLOCK * BLOCKS];
static void *free_list = NULL;
```

- `void pool_init(void)` links all 32 blocks into the free list, **block 0 first** (block i points to block i + 1, the last points to NULL)
- `void *pool_alloc(void)` pops the head of the free list (or returns NULL when empty)
- `void pool_free(void *p)` pushes `p` back onto the front of the list

Keep your bump allocator; the pool lives alongside it.
hints: Treat the start of each free block as a `void *` slot: `*(void **)block = next;`
Alloc pops: `p = free_list; free_list = *(void **)p;`. Free pushes: `*(void **)p = free_list; free_list = p;`

milestones.title: Safety checks
milestones.text:
Real allocators defend against misuse. Add:

- `int pool_owns(const void *p)`: 1 if `p` is the **start** of a block inside the pool, else 0
- `int pool_available(void)`: how many blocks are currently free (walk the list)
- make `pool_free` ignore pointers the pool doesn't own (do nothing)
hints: Convert addresses to `uintptr_t` (from `<stdint.h>`) to compare and subtract them safely.
Inside the pool and `(addr - start) % BLOCK == 0` means it's a block start.
